co_bauhaus_wall.blurb: A steep limestone wall tucked behind trees in the canyon at Rifle Mountain Park, near Rifle. All 26 climbs are bolted, and nothing here is easy: it begins at 5.11 and climbs through 5.12 and a big block of 5.13 to a handful of 5.14s. The far-left end holds the gentler lines plus a small bouldering cave, while the main section to the right is sustained and powerful, usually starting in a cave and finishing on a pocketed, tufa-streaked face with incut fins. Because few people climb here, expect some loose rock near the ground. A strong choice for experienced sport climbers chasing hard grades, and a poor one for anyone still working up through the 5.10s.
co_bauhaus_wall.parking_note: Leave the car in a pullout on the right of the canyon road, roughly eight-tenths of a mile beyond the park entrance.

co_alcove_the.blurb: A cool, sheltered sport sector of Ouray's Pool Wall, just north of town and reached by walking straight up the gully from the base of the cliff. Of its 26 routes, 25 are bolted and one is a top-rope line. Grades start around 5.5, include a good number of easier and middle-grade lines, bulk up through 5.9 to 5.11, and top out with a couple of 5.13s. The pale sandstone is technical, with small edges and gritty texture, and the walls hold shade better than the sectors around them, which helps on warm days. A decent pick for newer leaders and for mixed groups. Loose rock can drop from the alcove ceiling now and then, so wear a helmet.

co_upper_tier_bocco_area.blurb: The higher cliff band among the Wolcott crags, on the hillside above the camping flat near Wolcott and I-70. It holds 26 routes, about three-quarters of them bolted and the rest trad, on short Dakota sandstone walls. Difficulty runs from 5.6 up to a single 5.12, with most climbs landing between 5.8 and 5.10 and a few 5.11s. The wall catches sun for most of the day, so it suits cooler weather and can be a pleasant winter stop. The cliff is not heavily polished, and the walk up is longer than to the lower tier. Good for climbers at the moderate grades.
co_upper_tier_bocco_area.approach: Walk past the far end of the campsites, join the old rail line heading west, and after roughly half a mile take the hiker's trail up the hillside on the right to the base of the wall.

co_phantom_spire.blurb: A prominent sandstone spire and the wall beside it in Devil's Canyon, part of the McInnis Canyons country near Grand Junction. This is adventure climbing: of 26 routes, most are traditional, with a few aid lines and a single top-rope. Free grades run from about 5.6 to 5.12, with the bulk between 5.9 and 5.11. Some lines finish on the canyon rim while others are reached by rappelling in and climbing back out. Expect chimneys, towers and the occasional clean corner, with rock quality that varies from one line to the next. A rack, route-finding and comfort with committing approaches are needed, and it is not a spot for beginners.
co_phantom_spire.approach: Follow the main trail up the east side of the canyon and continue beyond the tower at the canyon mouth. The spire appears on your left.

co_great_black_north_the.blurb: A north-facing limestone sport crag at the far end of Shelf Road, near Canon City. All 26 routes are bolted, and the crag is known for stiff grades: a small handful of 5.9 to 5.11 lines, then a heavy block of 5.12s, with a few 5.13s and 5.14s at the top. Easier routes are scarce. The stone is generally solid and pocketed, though black lichen, some vegetation and a band of loose rock at the start of many lines are part of the deal, and first bolts tend to be high. Walls tilt slightly east and west, so some routes pick up morning or afternoon sun, and with few big trees it can feel exposed in summer. Quiet compared with the main Shelf cliffs.

co_rincon_center_route_r.blurb: A compact wall at the west end of Eldorado Canyon, near Boulder, with a reputation for dense, high-quality climbing. Of its 26 routes, nearly all are traditional; just a couple are bolted and one is a top-rope. Grades cover 5.8 to 5.12, but the heart of the wall is 5.10 and 5.11. Many lines are multipitch, serious and sparsely protected, so bring a full rack and good protection skills. The wall faces south, which makes it comfortable in cooler months and decent in early summer, and the views reach toward the Continental Divide. Nice weekends bring crowds. Descents are by rappel or gullies to either side.
co_rincon_center_route_r.approach: Take the trail that leaves the main canyon path at its far end, then pick your way up the talus field to the base of the wall.
